content:
I've been a huge Sonos fan and customer for years, going all the way back to the original Sonos One. So, when I heard about two years ago that Sonos was entering the over-ear headphone market, I knew I had to give them a try. The Sonos Ace looked great, felt comfortable to wear, and brought some really nice Sonos ecosystem features. But as a pair of high-end headphones, there were still a few things that left me less than satisfied, such as stronger bass, better active noise cancellation (ANC), and a better app experience. Now, however, the new Sonos Ace Ultra feels like they've gone down the checklist item by item, addressing almost all of the complaints from most customers (including me). I've been using these headphones as my main pair for almost a month, for flights, video editing, working out, walking, and everyday music listening. So I'm very familiar with them, and here's what you need to know.

Be sure to check out our Sonos Ace Ultra hands-on video review below:

At first glance, the Sonos Ace Ultra doesn't look all that different from the original Sonos Ace. They retain the same kind of clean, understated design, just with differently placed chrome accents and a few more colour options. But the biggest differences are on the inside of these headphones.

Comparison with the original Sonos Ace

Here are some of the biggest changes from the original Sonos Ace to the Ace Ultra:

  • Redesigned 40mm drivers
  • 10-microphone array, up from 8 on the previous generation
  • Improved adaptive active noise cancellation (ANC), claimed to be up to twice as effective, and able to automatically adjust to changes in glasses, hair, and the seal around the ears
  • Longer battery life, up to 35 hours with ANC on
  • Bluetooth 6.0, up from 5.4 on the previous generation
  • Expanded EQ controls, offering three presets plus an advanced 8-band EQ option
  • Headphones can be paired with the Sonos ecosystem
  • User-replaceable battery
  • Updated ear cushion and headband padding materials
  • Larger ear cup swivel angle, allowing them to lie flat when worn around the neck
  • Two new colours: Agave and Sand

Of these changes, the ones I noticed most were the redesigned acoustics, stronger bass performance, and more powerful ANC. With the original Sonos Ace in ANC mode, I would occasionally hear a slight hiss. It didn't happen often, but I did notice it. So far, the new Sonos Ace Ultra has already fixed this issue. Some of the standout features from the previous generation have been carried over, such as:

  • Spatial audio and Dolby Atmos
  • Dynamic head tracking
  • Lossless audio support on compatible devices
  • USB-C and 3.5mm wired audio input
  • Bluetooth multipoint connectivity
  • Fast charging, with 3 minutes of charging delivering up to 3 hours of playback
  • TV Audio Swap feature when paired with a compatible Sonos soundbar

They still maintain that same extremely high-quality build, combining plastic and metal to give you a premium, lightweight feel. The Sonos Ace Ultra also retains the magnetic, swappable ear cushions, and one of the coolest things I noticed is the all-new EQ settings, which really let me fine-tune the sound to exactly the way I like to listen. But as a pair of everyday headphones, how do they actually perform?

My experience using them

Specs are easy to write down on paper, but the thing I'm most impressed by with the Ace Ultra is that the sound is noticeably better. My biggest complaint about the original Sonos Ace was that it lacked low-end depth. The bass wasn't bad per se, but for a pair of $450 headphones, I felt it fell a little short. I listen to a lot of R&B, hip-hop, and pop, so bass matters a lot to me. I wanted more low-end punch, I wanted to feel that impact. The Ace Ultra finally gives me what I was looking for.

The low end is clearly more powerful and deeper. But one thing to note is that Sonos didn't just achieve this by cranking up the bass volume. Any headphone brand can turn up the bass, but the challenge is maintaining separation so the bass doesn't drown out the vocals, instruments, and highs. That's where the Ace Ultra really surprised me. The bass is stronger, yet the vocals remain clear and bright, and a pleasure to listen to. And it's not just for music; the sound is better across all media, such as podcasts, movies, and every YouTube video I watch. They perform brilliantly across every media use case.

The improvement in ANC is also immediately noticeable. The new 10-microphone array is able to dynamically push more sound away from the headphones. Even with no media playing, the headphones get to an incredibly quiet level in many different environments. It's seriously impressive! The biggest improvement in ANC is handling sudden bursts of noise. Blocking out constant noise like an aeroplane engine is one thing, but blocking out passing car sounds, construction noise, obvious alarms, or sudden loud noises while walking down the street is another.

The last two things I want to mention are comfort and the Sonos ecosystem. These are the most comfortable headphones I've ever worn. Even on long-haul flights of 8 to 10 hours, I wore them about 95% of the time without any soreness, discomfort, or stuffiness. Lastly, I have a lot of Sonos speakers at home, and they've added a new feature that lets you transfer music from the speakers to the headphones with a single tap. It's a great feature, but personally I don't use it all that much.

My only complaint is that the carrying case needs a new zipper or clasp design, because it constantly gets stuck on the sticker!

Pricing and availability

The Sonos Ace Ultra goes on sale today on the Sonos website and Amazon, priced at $449, the same launch price as the original Sonos Ace. It's available in four colours: Black, White, Agave, and Sand. I also noticed the original Sonos Ace is on clearance at Amazon for $239. At that $240 price point, it could still be a decent option.

At a $450 price point, the Sonos Ace Ultra sits firmly in the high-end noise-cancelling headphone tier, going head-to-head with options from Apple, Bose, and Sony.

Wrap-up

The original Sonos Ace felt like a decent first-generation product. The Sonos Ace Ultra feels like a complete, refined product. As we've seen, they didn't redesign the exterior, but they've improved things in all the important places, and even added a few new standout features. The sound is noticeably better, the ANC is stronger and smarter, the battery life is longer, the app experience is smoother, and that Agave colour is absolutely gorgeous.

If you already own the original Sonos Ace, I actually think there are enough reasons this time around to upgrade, depending on what matters most to you. If you're considering picking up a pair of high-end headphones, I think the Sonos Ace Ultra deserves a place on your shortlist. $449 is certainly not cheap, but if you want one of the best pairs of high-end headphones out there, and you're a Sonos fan, you're going to love these headphones.

What do you think? Have you tried the Sonos Ace lineup? Are you a Sonos customer? How do you find the app experience? Let's discuss in the comments below!
